claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the precursor-conversion rate relative to the atomic-diffusion rate.
Sufficiently rapid precursor conversion enforces simultaneous nucleation.
Sufficiently rapid precursor conversion kinetically suppresses atomic diffusion.
Simultaneous nucleation combined with suppressed diffusion produces a homogeneous, single-phase alloy.
The proposed initial state is a homogeneous dispersion of noble-metal salt precursors in a solvent under an inert atmosphere.
The controlled comparison uses an ultra-rapid, sub-second thermal pulse and a slightly extended heating pulse.
In situ monitoring will confirm complete precursor conversion during the ultra-rapid pulse.
The comparison holds chemical and ambient conditions constant while changing thermal-pulse duration.
Rapidly nucleated metal atoms become kinetically frozen before significant diffusion or phase segregation occurs.
Kinetic trapping of the metal atoms produces a homogeneous, high-entropy solid solution.
Slower heating provides enough time for local diffusion and thereby leads to phase separation.
Relative to the longer-pulse baseline, the ultra-rapid-pulse sample will be single-phase and uniformly mixed.
The ultra-rapid-pulse sample will retain high surface-atom exposure.
The longer-pulse sample will exhibit elemental segregation and phase inhomogeneity.
The hypothesis applies to liquid-phase noble-metal nanoparticle synthesis under inert atmospheres using compatible salt precursors.
Strong support binding or persistent coordinating agents may invalidate the proposed conversion–diffusion mechanism by altering nucleation or diffusion dynamics.
The critical pulse duration may vary with metal composition and experimental conditions.
Failure of the ultra-rapid pulse to improve homogeneity relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of a transition from homogeneous to phase-separated structures as pulse duration increases would falsify the hypothesis.
